When does conformal calibration need censoring weights?
Cause-of-failure prediction sets under competing risks

Sunny Yang guangy4@illinois.edu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Weiyan Zhao Affiliation: Northumbria University
Abstract

Split conformal prediction sets for competing-risks labels at a fixed horizon require calibration labels that right censoring can leave unobserved. Complete-case calibration guarantees coverage for the label-complete subpopulation, but its population coverage can deviate in either direction, even at the true class probabilities. We study how selection changes the score distribution near the population quantile. At the true score in our main simulation family, with independent draws, complete-case calibration covers 0.8723 at a nominal 0.900 when 22% of subjects are event-free at the horizon. In 4 of 48 further designs using per-draw normalisation, estimating cause incidences as one minus the exponential of the negative of the cause-specific Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazards, with the event-free probability as the clipped and renormalised remainder, puts complete-case coverage at least four standard errors below nominal. In these designs, weights from a correctly specified censoring model keep coverage near nominal. Extending the argument of Yi et al. (2025) to a cause label, we establish a finite-sample coverage lower bound with an explicit penalty for censoring-model error. Misspecifying the censoring model can also lead to under-coverage.

1 Introduction

For a competing-risks model, a natural prediction at a fixed horizon is a set of causes, possibly including event-free status, that contains the realised label at the horizon for at least 1−α1-\alpha of subjects. Split conformal prediction gives such a set from any fitted model when the calibration labels are observed. Under right censoring they are not, since a subject who leaves follow-up before the horizon without an event has no label.

Complete-case calibration keeps the subjects whose label is determined and drops the rest. It selects on the outcome, because a subject who fails early is more likely to have been followed long enough than one who survives past the horizon, and the exchangeability that conformal prediction relies on is lost. Boström et al. (2019) use this procedure for a binary event-by-horizon label and state its guarantee for the subjects not censored before the horizon. Boström et al. (2023) keep the censored subjects, with a Kaplan–Meier estimate within each Mondrian category, to give a predictive distribution for the event time. Reports on the population disagree. Dang et al. (2026) find complete-case conformal under-covering, attribute it to the censoring rate and recommend a switch above 40%. Farina et al. (2026) find their complete-case comparator over-covering in every setting they run, but their target is a lower prediction bound on the event time, for which selection toward short observed times is conservative by construction. Neither account applies to a label at a horizon.

We characterise when complete-case calibration is safe for a cause-of-failure label and when weighting the calibration sample by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored repairs it. The paper makes three contributions.

  1. 1.

    The complete-case error can take either sign, even at the true score. Complete-case calibration takes its threshold from the score distribution of the selected subjects, and we study how this selection changes coverage over the population. At fixed covariates, subjects event-free at the horizon have the lowest selection probability, so the event-free share, error in the fitted event-free probability and the dependence of censoring on the covariates all shift the selected score distribution relative to the population’s. The direction of the mean score shift indicates the sign of the error but does not determine it (Appendix F). In our main simulation family at the true score, the unweighted procedure over-covers at an event-free share of 0.5440.544 and under-covers at 0.2240.224, where it covers 0.87230.8723 at a nominal 0.9000.900 over 200200 replications with independent draws (Section 4.1). In a two-region law where most subjects are event-free, the true score still under-covers (Section 4.3). A fit that understates the event-free probability lowers coverage, censoring amplifies both effects, and the observed crossing point moves with the censoring rate, so no threshold on the censoring rate locates the failure. Estimating each cause’s incidence as one minus a cause-specific survival curve, with the event-free probability as the remainder, puts the unweighted procedure at least four standard errors below nominal in 4 of 48 designs (Section 4.2).

  2. 2.

    Censoring weights give a coverage guarantee for any score when the censoring model is correct. In the studied designs with covariate-free censoring, where the marginal Kaplan–Meier estimator is correctly specified, the weighted procedure stays within 0.0120.012 of nominal across event-free shares, misspecification levels and miscoverage levels. When censoring depends on the covariates, marginal Kaplan–Meier weights fail with the unweighted procedure, at 0.82940.8294 in a two-region law where region-stratified weights cover 0.94960.9496, and miss in either direction under a misspecified score, while weights from the true censoring model hold (Section 4.3). Table 1 summarises the four cases.

  3. 3.

    A finite-sample coverage floor for the weighted procedure. Lemma 1 establishes weighted exchangeability between the label-complete calibration sample and the test subject, and Theorem 1 gives a floor of 1−α−Δw1-\alpha-\Delta_{w} with Δw\Delta_{w} explicit in the censoring-model error. The argument is the factorisation of Yi et al. (2025, Appendix A) applied to the selection event {C≥min(T,t⋆)}\{C\geq\min(T,t^{\star})\} in place of {T≤C}\{T\leq C\}, with the normalising constant κ\kappa kept explicit and the random size of the complete-case pool accounted for. The cause label changes one step. A hypothesised time determines the test subject’s weight, but a hypothesised cause leaves min⁡(T,t⋆)\min(T,t^{\star}) unknown, so the procedure uses a dominating substitute for that weight, the atom.

The class-conditional procedure, which restores coverage of a rare cause that a pooled threshold misses, is in Section A.1, with a registry cohort of 238,057238{,}057 subjects.

Related work.

Conformal prediction under covariate shift is due to Tibshirani et al. (2019), the penalty for an estimated shift ratio to Lei and Candès (2021), and class-conditional, or Mondrian, conformal prediction to Vovk et al. Podkopaev and Ramdas (2021) reweight conformal classification under label shift. Their weight q⁡(y)/p⁡(y)q(y)/p(y) depends on the class index alone, so a hypothesised label determines the test weight, and their calibration set is fully labelled. Our weight 1/G⁡(min⁡(T,t⋆)∣X)1/G(\min(T,t^{\star})\mid X) depends on the subject’s event time, which a hypothesised cause leaves unknown. With estimated ratios their statement becomes asymptotic, whereas Theorem 1 keeps a finite-sample floor at an explicit cost Δw\Delta_{w}.

For survival outcomes, the closest in mechanism is Yi et al. (2025), who weight by the inverse probability of censoring with an outcome-dependent weight, and their Theorem 1 is a finite-sample floor minus a censoring-model term. They predict a time and invert a pp-value over candidate values, so the hypothesised object determines the test weight. Shin et al. (2025) add a covariate-shift ratio to this weight for an event-time interval, without a coverage theorem for the combined weight. Candès, Lei and Ren (2023) require Type-I censoring with the censoring time observed on every unit, and the PAC-type guarantees of Gui, Hore, Ren and Barber (2024) do not apply under loss to follow-up. Davidov et al. (2025) extend double robustness to general right censoring with a finite-sample bound whose slack in the weight-estimation error is of the same kind as ours; their bound is a lower bound on a single survival time, holds with probability 1−δ1-\delta over the calibration data rather than marginally, and does not treat a cause. Sesia and Svetnik (2025a) handle general right censoring by imputation, and Farina et al. (2026), Qin et al. (2025) and Si and Qiu (2025) give asymptotic guarantees. Holmes and Marandon (2025) give a finite-sample two-sided interval on the subjects that a trained classifier assigns to the uncensored population. Alberge et al. (2025), Wang et al. (2026) and Dang et al. (2026) address the cause or the fold restriction with, respectively, a point prediction, an asymptotic interval, and a finite-sample statement that assumes the exchangeability at issue. Sesia and Svetnik (2025b, 2026) form conformal pp-values from inverse-probability-of-censoring weights on uncensored subjects, for survival thresholds and for selecting patients event-free past a horizon, with asymptotic false discovery rate control and a finite-sample version whose slack is of order n−1/2n^{-1/2} (2025b, Theorem 5).

For missing and coarsened outcomes, Paul et al. (2025) calibrate a prediction set for a real outcome from monotonely coarsened data through the efficient influence function, with finite-sample validity when some nuisance functions are known. Their threshold takes an infimum over the data consistent with the test covariates, which is the nearest precedent for the atom of (3). Yin, Shi, Wang and Blei (2024) and Jin, Ren and Candès (2023) give the test slot the upper bound of a response-dependent likelihood ratio, and Yi, Zhang, Tang and Wang (in press) keep a finite-sample floor under nonignorable missingness with a response-dependent propensity. In both, a hypothesised response determines its weight. Fan et al. (2025) keep finite-sample coverage under missing covariates with a response-dependent likelihood ratio, but the response is always observed. A conservative finite-sample guarantee for a set of causes follows by set inclusion from the partial-label construction of Javanmardi et al. (2023, Theorem 1), which calibrates on each subject’s largest score over the labels consistent with its data; a subject censored before the horizon is consistent with every label and enters calibration at its largest score. Liu, de Paula and Tamer (2025) follow a related conservative route for interval-valued outcomes. The guarantee here calibrates on the label-complete subjects and pays only for the censoring-model error.

2 Problem and procedures

Fix a horizon t⋆>0t^{\star}>0. A subject has covariates X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X}, a latent first event time T>0T>0 and a cause ε∈{1,…,K}\varepsilon\in\{1,\dots,K\}. The quantity to be predicted is the horizon label

Y={ε,T≤t⋆,0,T>t⋆,Y∈{0,1,…,K},Y\;=\;\begin{cases}\varepsilon,&T\leq t^{\star},\\ 0,&T>t^{\star},\end{cases}\qquad Y\in\{0,1,\dots,K\},

which records the cause of the first event by t⋆t^{\star}, or event-free status. Right censoring at time CC gives the observed follow-up T~=min⁡(T,C)\widetilde{T}=\min(T,C). The label is determined, and we call the subject label-complete, exactly on the event

Δ≔ 1{C≥m},m≔min(T,t⋆),\Delta\;\coloneqq\;\mathbf{1}\{\,C\geq m\,\},\qquad m\;\coloneqq\;\min(T,t^{\star}),

since a subject followed to mm either has had the event, with its cause recorded, or is known to be event-free at t⋆t^{\star}.

Let πℓ​(x)∈[0,1]\pi_{\ell}(x)\in[0,1], ℓ∈{0,…,K}\ell\in\{0,\dots,K\}, be fitted class probabilities at t⋆t^{\star}, obtained from cause-specific cumulative incidence increments and the event-free probability of a model trained on an independent split 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}. The nonconformity score is

s⁡(x,ℓ)= 1−πℓ​(x),V=s⁡(X,Y)= 1−πY​(X),s(x,\ell)\;=\;1-\pi_{\ell}(x),\qquad V\;=\;s(X,Y)\;=\;1-\pi_{Y}(X),

{Y∈Sq(X)}={V≤q}.\{Y\in S_{q}(X)\}\;=\;\{V\leq q\}. (1)

The score depends on the subject only through (X,Y)(X,Y).

Write G⁡(u∣x)=ℙ⁡(C≥u∣X=x)G(u\mid x)=\mathbb{P}(C\geq u\mid X=x) for the conditional censoring survival function, taken throughout with a closed inequality. A marginal G⁡(u)G(u) is the special case of an XX-free GG. The oracle inverse-probability-of-censoring weight and its plug-in are

w⋆=1G⁡(m∣X),w^=1G^​(m∣X),w^{\star}\;=\;\frac{1}{G(m\mid X)},\qquad\widehat{w}\;=\;\frac{1}{\widehat{G}(m\mid X)},

with G^\widehat{G} fitted on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} and therefore independent of the calibration and test subjects. In the implementation G^\widehat{G} is floored at gming_{\min} before inversion, so w^≤1/gmin\widehat{w}\leq 1/g_{\min} by construction and the conditioning event of Theorem 1 holds. Positivity bounds the oracle weights, while the floor bounds the estimated ones. Clipping an unbounded weight is a different problem (Wang and Goel, 2026).

From a calibration sample of i.i.d. subjects, keep the label-complete ones, ℐ={i:Δi=1}\mathcal{I}=\{i:\Delta_{i}=1\}, with scores ViV_{i} and weights w^i\widehat{w}_{i}. Define a self-normalised weighted quantile carrying an atom of mass AA at +∞+\infty. With pi=w^i/(∑j∈ℐw^j+A)p_{i}=\widehat{w}_{i}/(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\widehat{w}_{j}+A),

q^=inf{q:∑i∈ℐpi 1{Vi≤q}≥ 1−α},\widehat{q}\;=\;\inf\Big\{q:\ \textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}p_{i}\,\mathbf{1}\{V_{i}\leq q\}\ \geq\ 1-\alpha\Big\}, (2)

and output Sq^​(X)S_{\widehat{q}}(X) for a fresh subject.

Two procedures are compared throughout. The weighted procedure runs (2) with the weights w^i\widehat{w}_{i} and the atom of (3) below. The unweighted, or complete-case, procedure sets every weight and the atom to 11, which is split conformal prediction on the label-complete subjects. It carries no guarantee for the full population under this selection, since Δ=𝟏{C≥min(T,t⋆)}\Delta=\mathbf{1}\{C\geq\min(T,t^{\star})\} depends on the outcome through TT.

The atom is where predicting a cause departs from weighted conformal prediction. Lemma 1 puts the test subject’s own weight on the test slot, and that weight depends on the unobserved m=min⁡(T,t⋆)m=\min(T,t^{\star}), so it cannot be computed at prediction time. The procedure uses a dominating substitute (Lemma 3),

Aenv=1max⁡{G^​(t⋆∣X),gmin}≥w^te,A_{\mathrm{env}}\;=\;\frac{1}{\max\{\widehat{G}(t^{\star}\mid X),\,g_{\min}\}}\;\geq\;\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{te}}, (3)

which uses no test outcome. Atom mass can only raise the quantile, so any dominating substitute preserves the coverage floor.

4 Experiments

Covariates are independent standard normals, cause-specific hazards are constant with cause 1 depending on the first covariate, the horizon is t⋆=1t^{\star}=1 and the all-cause survival there is 0.50.5 at zero signal (the share parameter). Censoring is exponential and, unless a design states otherwise, covariate-free, so coverage is computed against the generating process’s own censoring survival and the evaluation shares no estimate with the procedure. The designs use gmin=0.05g_{\min}=0.05, between 2.52.5 and 1717 times looser than Assumption 2 permits in them; designs with another value state it in their captions. Section C gives the remaining constants.

Section 4.1 holds the fitted model correct, Section 4.2 misspecifies it in a controlled direction, and Section 4.3 keeps the score exact and misspecifies the censoring model, covering three cells of Table 1.

4.1 A correctly specified score

Table 2 runs the unweighted procedure at the true class probabilities. The share parameter 0.50.5, 0.250.25 and 0.150.15 gives realised event-free shares of 0.5440.544, 0.3220.322 and 0.2240.224. At the largest share the unweighted procedure over-covers, increasingly with censoring, from 0.90560.9056 at censoring 0.200.20 to 0.93720.9372 at 0.750.75. At the smallest it under-covers, at 0.87740.8774. The weighted procedure stays between 0.90060.9006 and 0.90960.9096. That table normalises each draw by its own covariate mean and averages 2020 replications, so the calibration pool and the test draw do not share one law exactly. With a fixed normaliser, so that all subjects are i.i.d., and 200200 replications (Table 10), the smallest share covers 0.87230.8723, 2121 standard errors below nominal, the middle share 0.90080.9008, within one standard error of nominal, and the largest share 0.90530.9053 to 0.93800.9380 across censoring rates, while the weighted procedure stays between 0.90050.9005 and 0.90540.9054.

Figure 1 shows the mechanism. The unweighted threshold is a quantile of the label-complete scores, and selection shifts their distribution relative to the population’s near 1−α1-\alpha. Subjects event-free at the horizon have the lowest selection probability at fixed covariates and are under-represented in complete-case calibration. At a large share the true score ranks their label as the easiest, and under-representing them raises the threshold. At a small share it ranks their label among the hardest, and under-representing them lowers it.

A fitted forest overstates the event-free probability, by 0.0270.027 at the largest share and 0.1600.160 at the smallest, which pushes the unweighted procedure up. At a fitted score the unweighted procedure therefore does not fall below nominal across censoring rates, event-free shares and miscoverage levels (Figure 4 and Appendix K). At the true score the censoring and miscoverage-level sweeps still over-cover, with the smallest margin 0.95490.9549 against 0.9500.950 (e53-cells.json), and the event-free-share sweep under-covers as above.

At a fitted score, Figure 4 crosses the miscoverage level with the censoring rate over 16 cells, and the weighted procedure returns sets no larger than the unweighted ones in all 16. The arms share seeds, forest and splits, so the differences are paired, and all 16 are negative. Relative to the unweighted set the reduction ranges from 0.52%0.52\% at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and censoring 0.20.2, where it is −0.0134±0.0020-0.0134\pm 0.0020 labels, to 25.5%25.5\% at α=0.3\alpha=0.3 and censoring 0.750.75. Appendix K compares both procedures with a set read directly off the fitted cumulative incidence functions.

4.2 A misspecified score

To misspecify the fitted model in a known direction we shrink its event-free probability by a factor 1−b1-b and renormalise. The shrinkage is applied to the forest’s output, so no forest is refitted and the misspecification is separate from the covariate noise that Table 15 varies. The origin b=0b=0 is the forest, not the truth. In the exponential family the forest’s mean event-free probability exceeds the true one by up to 0.0720.072 at censoring 0.700.70 (Table 2), so the crossings below are measured from a slight overstatement. Coverage is weighted by the oracle GG, so an error in G^\hat{G} cannot offset itself.

Table 3 crosses bb with the censoring rate. At b=0b=0 the unweighted procedure’s over-coverage grows with censoring, from +0.0020+0.0020 to +0.0039+0.0039 at censoring 0.200.20 to +0.0263+0.0263 to +0.0318+0.0318 at 0.700.70, as in Section 4.1 under a different generator. The coverage loss caused by bb also grows with censoring, from −0.0061-0.0061 to −0.0082-0.0082 at 0.200.20 to −0.0422-0.0422 to −0.0687-0.0687 at 0.700.70, a factor of 7.07.0 to 8.88.8 with paired standard errors of 2.02.0 and 2.72.7.

Censoring thus amplifies two effects of opposite sign: the over-coverage at b=0b=0 and the loss from a misspecified fit. At b=0b=0 the unweighted procedure is above nominal by at least 2 marginal standard errors in 11 of the 12 cells. At b=0.6b=0.6 it is below nominal in every cell, by that margin in 11, so at every censoring rate the procedure crosses nominal at some intermediate bb, and the crossing point varies with the censoring rate. At 250250 replications (Table 18), non-PH at b=0.4b=0.4 covers 0.89710.8971 at censoring 0.400.40, 4.54.5 standard errors below nominal, and 0.91950.9195 at 0.700.70. Weibull at b=0.5b=0.5 covers 0.89400.8940 and 0.90310.9031, 9.59.5 below and 2.92.9 above. Within one family and at a fixed misspecification, raising the censoring rate moves the procedure from below nominal to above it. The observed crossing point moves with the censoring rate (Table 17, Figure 2), so no threshold on the censoring rate alone separates safe from unsafe cases. The weighted procedure ranges from 0.89710.8971 to 0.90750.9075 across the grid.

Where the error lands.

Table 19 decomposes the unweighted procedure’s miscoverage by true label. Subjects event-free at the horizon have m=t⋆m=t^{\star}, so their selection probability is G⁡(t⋆)G(t^{\star}), the smallest possible, and the calibration fold is depleted of them. At censoring 0.700.70 their selection rate is 0.19600.1960, against 0.56040.5604 and 0.53320.5332 for the two causes. At b=0b=0 the unweighted procedure covers this group 0.99950.9995 of the time and all of its error falls on the cause labels. At b=0.6b=0.6 the group carries +0.0700+0.0700 of additional miscoverage while both causes improve.

Since bb raises the event-free group’s nonconformity by construction, we compare with a control λ\lambda that replaces the informative covariate with noise in training. It changes the fitted model, taking cause-2 coverage from 0.82820.8282 to 0.77260.7726, but leaves the event-free group’s miscoverage at 0.00000.0000, a change of −0.0003-0.0003 from the b=0b=0 row. A misspecification that leaves the depleted group alone does not move marginal coverage. The effect also scales with the depletion: the same bb adds +0.0165+0.0165 of miscoverage at censoring 0.400.40 and +0.0430+0.0430 at 0.700.70, while the event-free selection rate falls from 0.63310.6331 to 0.19600.1960.

A common misspecification.

A standard competing-risks error acts in the same direction as bb. Estimating each cause’s incidence as one minus a cause-specific survival curve treats the competing event as censoring and understates the event-free probability. We ran this error in all three families over 48 designs at 100 replications each, taking each cause’s curve as one minus the exponential of the negative of the forest’s cause-specific Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard and the event-free probability as one minus their sum, clipped and renormalised (Table 21). The equivalent bb reaches 0.17640.1764 under exponential hazards, 0.24640.2464 under Weibull and 0.30880.3088 under non-proportional hazards. These designs use per-draw normalisation and, for Weibull and non-proportional hazards, a censoring rate set from each draw (Appendix C). The unweighted procedure falls at least two standard errors below nominal in 7 designs, all Weibull or non-proportional at censoring 0.200.20 to 0.550.55, and at least four standard errors below in 4, at censoring 0.200.20 to 0.400.40. The lowest coverage is 0.89200.8920, under non-proportional hazards at censoring 0.400.40 and competing fraction 0.60.6. In a paired comparison on the exponential family (Table 20) the weighted procedure does not move with the error, at tt between −1.1-1.1 and +0.9+0.9 in all 8 cells, while the unweighted procedure falls significantly in 7 of them and stays above nominal. Whether this error alone breaks unweighted calibration depends on the hazard shape rather than on the size of the error.

Public cohorts.

Three competing-risks cohorts from the R package survival show the same direction. Their censoring depends on the covariates, and in these analyses coverage is estimated with the marginal Kaplan–Meier model that the weighted procedure also calibrates on, so the estimates do not establish population coverage. Under this estimator the unweighted procedure as fitted is estimated above nominal in all 6 cells, by 0.0030.003 to 0.0290.029. At b=0.6b=0.6 the estimated coverage at the later horizon is 0.89130.8913 for mgus2 and 0.89660.8966 for PBC. These estimates use a misspecified censoring model, and the mgus2 cell also violates Assumption 2 in the latest quarter of accrual (Section D.1).

4.3 A misspecified censoring model

The weighted procedure is robust to errors in the score only if its weights are correct. Figure 3 and Table 8 make censoring depend on the covariate that carries the signal, on bounded support so that G⁡(t⋆∣X)≥0.08G(t^{\star}\mid X)\geq 0.08 for every subject, and use the oracle score so that the only error is in G^\widehat{G}. The unweighted procedure stays above nominal, lowest at 0.90080.9008. Marginal Kaplan–Meier weights are at least two standard errors below nominal in 4 of the 6 designs with covariate-dependent censoring, at 0.89460.8946 to 0.89880.8988, while Kaplan–Meier within 10 bins of the covariate holds at 0.90060.9006 or above. The shortfalls are small and in the direction Theorem 1 allows, since a marginal G^\widehat{G} is misspecified once censoring depends on the covariates and Δw\Delta_{w} is then positive.

Stronger covariate dependence breaks both procedures. In a two-region law with the true score, 40%40\% of subjects are in a region where 30%30\% are event-free at the horizon and G⁡(t⋆)=0.10G(t^{\star})=0.10, and the rest in a region where 95%95\% are event-free and G⁡(t⋆)=0.90G(t^{\star})=0.90. The unweighted procedure and marginal Kaplan–Meier weights both cover 0.82940.8294 with single-label sets, while Kaplan–Meier weights fitted within each region and the oracle weights cover 0.94960.9496 with 1.401.40 labels (e54-cells.json, 200 replications). Complete-case selection retains the region-B survivors, whose label the true score ranks easiest, and drops the region-A survivors, whose label it ranks among the hardest, so the complete-case threshold is too small. Marginal weights cannot undo selection between regions. Most subjects, 0.690.69, are event-free at the horizon, and the true score still under-covers, so the event-free share of Section 4.1 indicates where selection moves the scores but does not determine it.

The right two panels of Figure 3 (Table 9) also misspecify the score, shrinking the true event-free probability by 1−b1-b in the design of Table 8. The unweighted procedure misses in either direction: at b=0.6b=0.6 it covers 0.83490.8349 when censoring is heavier where cause 1 is likelier (γ=3\gamma=3) and 0.91980.9198 when it leans the other way. Marginal Kaplan–Meier weights follow it, from 0.84130.8413 to 0.92690.9269. Oracle weights stay between 0.89920.8992 and 0.90090.9009, and binned Kaplan–Meier weights within 0.00120.0012 of nominal except one cell at 0.89750.8975 (e55-cells.json).

Real covariates.

Table 11 keeps the covariates and fitted covariate effects of two public cohorts, mgus2 and PBC, takes a cause-specific exponential regression fitted to each as the truth, and adds synthetic censoring that depends on each subject’s true all-cause hazard, so the true GG is known. Weights from the true GG, or from binned Kaplan–Meier, stay between 0.89950.8995 and 0.90300.9030 in all 1212 cells. At the true score and γ=+3\gamma=+3, the unweighted procedure on mgus2 covers 0.88850.8885 and marginal Kaplan–Meier weights 0.88710.8871, while binned Kaplan–Meier covers 0.90180.9018, so the upper-right cell of Table 1 also appears on real covariates. On PBC at the true score with covariate-free censoring the unweighted procedure over-covers, at 0.92030.9203, and an understated event-free probability lowers it by 0.02580.0258 on mgus2 and 0.03270.0327 on PBC, as in Section 4.2. Under a misspecified score it again misses in either direction, from 0.86110.8611 to 0.92060.9206 (e58-cells.json).

Outside positivity.

When Assumption 2 fails, coverage degrades gradually. In a design where only the population mass pp whose true G⁡(t⋆∣X)G(t^{\star}\mid X) equals half of gming_{\min} varies, coverage against the latent label is 0.8980.898, 0.8960.896, 0.8940.894 and 0.8830.883 as pp goes from 00 to 0.300.30, and on the violating subjects themselves 0.8950.895, 0.8760.876 and 0.8260.826 (Table 14). The clip at gming_{\min} cannot detect this: it acts on the analyst’s estimate, and a marginal Kaplan–Meier averages over the hard region, so the clip fires at rate 0.00000.0000 at every pp, including the one where 3030 per cent of subjects are below the bound. Reweighting cannot repair a violated identity.

5 Discussion and limitations

In the studied simulation families, a correct outcome model does not protect the unweighted procedure. At the true score it under-covers when few subjects are event-free at the horizon, and under covariate-dependent censoring it can fail badly. A fit that understates the event-free probability lowers coverage at any censoring rate, and whether the total crosses nominal depends jointly on the share, the size of the error, the censoring rate and the hazard shape. In these designs, weights from a correct censoring model kept the weighted procedure near nominal across all of these, and it is the only one of the two procedures with a guarantee, conditional on G^\widehat{G}. With a misspecified censoring model it fails with the unweighted procedure, and marginal Kaplan–Meier weights fall below nominal in 4 of the 6 covariate-dependent designs of Table 8. In these synthetic and semi-synthetic designs the practical question is whether the censoring can be modelled, not whether the outcome model is good. On SEER at t⋆=107t^{\star}=107 months, the one real censoring mechanism studied, correcting the censoring model changed pooled coverage by 0.00110.0011, and the marginal model was closer to nominal (Section D).

The cells of Table 1 come from different designs. Section 4.2 uses a fitted forest and covariate-free censoring, and Section 4.3 the true score and covariate-dependent censoring, so their magnitudes are not comparable. The synthetic designs outside Section 4.3 share one structure: independent Gaussian covariates, a cause-1 signal on the first covariate and covariate-free exponential censoring, with three hazard families. The real-covariate design of Table 11 departs from it, but its event times are exponential and its censoring synthetic.

The bound on Δw\Delta_{w} is a total-variation coupling with a gmin−2g_{\min}^{-2} constant. It exceeds α=0.1\alpha=0.1 in every design we run, while the measured Δw\Delta_{w} ranges from 0.00350.0035 to 0.23710.2371, so it establishes the parametric rate in ∥G^−G∥\lVert\widehat{G}-G\rVert but gives no usable number. The penalty is a population quantity in the unknown GG and cannot be estimated from the data.

The shrinkage bb is applied to the fitted model’s output rather than obtained by fitting a different model, and at b=0.6b=0.6 it understates the event-free rate by a factor of 2.52.5 in the cell that crosses. The competing-risks error of Section 4.2 reaches the crossing without shrinkage, under two of the three hazard families. Fitted-score experiments use a competing-risks forest, except Table 16, and oracle-score experiments use the known class probabilities. Standard errors on the public cohorts are over splits of one fixed sample, so those rows describe the procedure on those cohorts.

Reproducibility statement

The code that produced every table and figure accompanies the submission, with the fixed seeds of each experiment. The tables report runs at the atom (3), except two tables in Appendix K, the corner design, which uses oracle weights and the constant atom 1/gmin1/g_{\min}, and the per-class thresholds of the independence-violation design, which use the constant atom. Assumptions 1 to 3 are stated in Section 2, and every proof is in Section E. The simulation designs, their constants and the number of replications behind each exhibit are in Section C. Table entries are generated from the run outputs rather than transcribed.

SEER data are released under a data-use agreement that does not permit redistribution, so the registry cohort cannot accompany this paper. We provide the selection statement that defines it, the two filters and their sensitivity analyses (Section D), and the aggregate outputs behind every registry number in the text. A reader holding a SEER release can rebuild the cohort from the stated selection.

Ethics statement

The registry analysis uses the SEER public-use research data, which are de-identified at source and obtained under the standard data-use agreement. No individual-level record is reported here and no subject is identifiable from any aggregate in this paper. The work is a methodological study of uncertainty quantification and was not used to guide the care of any patient.

Generative AI disclosure

An AI coding assistant (Anthropic’s Claude, used through Claude Code) assisted with implementing the experiments and with preparing this manuscript. The research questions, the methodology and the final content of every claim were decided by the authors, who reviewed all AI-assisted output and take full responsibility for the correctness of the code and the accuracy of the claims.

Appendix A Oracle weights, the atom and per-cause thresholds

This section collects the parts of the theory the experiments do not turn on. The first is the floor at oracle weights, which Theorem 1 extends to estimated ones.

Lemma 2 (Oracle weights).

Run (2) with oracle calibration weights wi⋆w^{\star}_{i} and any atom AA that dominates the test slot’s own weight, A≥wte⋆A\geq w^{\star}_{\mathrm{te}} almost surely. Under Assumptions 1 to 3,

ℙ⁡(Y∈Sq^​(X))≥ 1−α.\mathbb{P}\big(Y\in S_{\widehat{q}}(X)\big)\;\geq\;1-\alpha.

The constant w∞=1/gminw_{\infty}=1/g_{\min} is such an atom by Assumption 2, and so is the smaller 1/G⁡(t⋆∣X)1/G(t^{\star}\mid X) (Remark A3).

Proof.

In Section E. ∎

Lemma 3 (Which weight the atom must dominate).

Theorem 1 and Corollary 2 hold for any atom AA with A≥w^teA\geq\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{te}} almost surely, where w^te\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{te}} is the calibration weight function the procedure itself uses, evaluated at the test subject. This is one rule and not two, Lemma 2 being its case w^=w⋆\widehat{w}=w^{\star}. Two atoms qualify, both computable and neither adding a condition to the theorem.

  1. (i)

    The envelope AenvA_{\mathrm{env}} of (3), whenever G^(⋅∣X)\widehat{G}(\cdot\mid X) is non-increasing in its time argument, which is a property of the estimator, required here rather than assumed of GG, and holding whenever G^\widehat{G} is one minus a non-decreasing cumulative estimate, as both estimators run in this paper are. Given it, m≤t⋆m\leq t^{\star} gives max⁡{G^​(t⋆∣X),gmin}≤max⁡{G^​(m∣X),gmin}=1/w^te\max\{\widehat{G}(t^{\star}\mid X),g_{\min}\}\leq\max\{\widehat{G}(m\mid X),g_{\min}\}=1/\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{te}}. The same G^\widehat{G} stands on both sides, which is what makes this an identity rather than a statistical claim. An envelope built from a different estimator than the one supplying the weights carries no such guarantee, and the second and third rows of Table 4 measure what that costs.

  2. (ii)

    The constant w∞=1/gminw_{\infty}=1/g_{\min}, because the implementation clips G^\widehat{G} at gming_{\min} before inversion, so w^≤1/gmin\widehat{w}\leq 1/g_{\min} identically and no event is involved here either. The clip satisfies the conditioning event of Theorem 1 by construction.

Since Aenv≤w∞A_{\mathrm{env}}\leq w_{\infty} always, (i) is the better of the two, and (ii) is the one admissible under the oracle weights as well.

Proof.

In Section E. ∎

Which target is meant decides whether the proof applies, and Table 4 measures it. Domination is checked on every label-complete test subject under covariate-dependent censoring, for three atoms against both candidate targets. Every construction changes verdict with the target. The shipped envelope never violates the weight the procedure carries but does violate the oracle weight, and the two atoms whose estimator is not the one supplying the weights are exactly the other way round. It is the first column that Theorem 1 requires. Those two rows are the failure the lemma rules out. They use the true GG, which carries no estimation error, so what breaks domination is the mismatch and not a deficiency of the atom’s own estimate. An analyst whose weights come from a conditional estimate while the envelope is read off a marginal one stands in the same relation and holds no oracle.

Remark A1 (An operating condition at small α\alpha).

The atom is not free at small α\alpha. The weighted quantile targets (1−α)​(W+A)(1-\alpha)(W+A) with W=∑i∈ℐw^iW=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\widehat{w}_{i} and AA the atom, so the threshold is +∞+\infty, and the prediction set is the whole label space, exactly when

W<A​1−αα.W\;<\;A\,\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}.

This is the classical split-conformal degeneracy n<1/α−1n<1/\alpha-1 with the atom’s mass in place of the sample size. Censoring enters only through AA. At (3) the boundary is small and set by the data, not by the analyst. Section F gives the check to run before forming a set.

Choose gming_{\min} before the data, from the design or from G^\widehat{G} on the training fold with a stated margin. Revising it upward after seeing WW is the move to avoid, since gming_{\min} is what Assumption 2 needs in order to bound GG from below. Sections B and F read these results further.

A.1 Per-cause thresholds

The same construction can be run once per label. For each ℓ∈{0,…,K}\ell\in\{0,\dots,K\} let ℐℓ={i∈ℐ:Yi=ℓ}\mathcal{I}_{\ell}=\{i\in\mathcal{I}:Y_{i}=\ell\} be the label-complete calibration subjects whose realised label is ℓ\ell, let q^ℓ\widehat{q}_{\ell} be (2) computed on ℐℓ\mathcal{I}_{\ell} alone with the same atom AA, and put

SM​(x)={ℓ:s⁡(x,ℓ)≤q^ℓ}.S^{\mathrm{M}}(x)\;=\;\{\ell:\ s(x,\ell)\leq\widehat{q}_{\ell}\}. (4)

This is the class-conditional, or Mondrian, form of the procedure, due in the uncensored setting to Vovk et al. Its guarantee is per class rather than pooled, and Corollary 2 states what censoring does to it.

Corollary 2 (Per-class coverage).

Run the per-class procedure (4) with estimated weights and the atom AenvA_{\mathrm{env}}, with G^\widehat{G} floored at gming_{\min} and non-increasing as in Theorem 1. Under Assumptions 1 to 3, for every label ℓ\ell with ℙ⁡(Y=ℓ)>0\mathbb{P}(Y=\ell)>0, conditionally on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} and on the event {G^≥gmin}\{\widehat{G}\geq g_{\min}\},

ℙ⁡(Y∈SM​(X)|Y=ℓ,𝒟tr)≥ 1−α−Δw(ℓ),Δw(ℓ)=12​κℓ​𝔼​[|GG^−κℓ||Y=ℓ],\mathbb{P}\big(Y\in S^{\mathrm{M}}(X)\,\big|\,Y=\ell,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}\big)\;\geq\;1-\alpha-\Delta_{w}^{(\ell)},\qquad\Delta_{w}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\frac{1}{2\kappa_{\ell}}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big|\frac{G}{\widehat{G}}-\kappa_{\ell}\Big|\,\Big|\,Y=\ell\Big],

with κℓ=𝔼⁡[G/G^∣Y=ℓ]\kappa_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[G/\widehat{G}\mid Y=\ell]. The supremum-norm bound of Theorem 1 holds with its expectation taken over XX given Y=ℓY=\ell, since κℓ≥𝔼⁡[G∣Y=ℓ]≥gmin\kappa_{\ell}\geq\mathbb{E}[G\mid Y=\ell]\geq g_{\min}.

Proof.

In Section E. ∎

The conditioning is on the realised label, not known at prediction time, so the guarantee is about the subgroup of subjects who turn out to have label ℓ\ell and not a selection rule. The per-class thresholds inherit the operating condition of Remark A1 one group at a time, so a class with Wℓ<A⁡(1−α)/αW_{\ell}<A(1-\alpha)/\alpha has q^ℓ=+∞\widehat{q}_{\ell}=+\infty and satisfies the corollary by entering every set.

A pooled coverage figure can sit at nominal while a rare cause is badly missed. Table 7 makes one cause rare, at 0.150.15 of events, and runs on oracle calibration weights at the uniform constant atom, so it isolates the per-cause effect from the censoring model. Pooled coverage reads 0.9020.902 while the decomposition under that single threshold is 0.9200.920 for the common cause, 0.9940.994 for event-free and 0.1180.118 for the rare one. Per-cause thresholds move every class to nominal, the common cause to 0.9020.902, the rare one to 0.9140.914 and event-free to 0.9030.903, at a mean set size of 2.422.42 against 1.841.84. Below the boundary of Remark A1 a class threshold is infinite and its per-cause coverage is the whole label space, so WℓW_{\ell} has to be reported with it.

The same gap appears on a SEER breast cancer cohort of 238,057238{,}057 subjects with two causes of death, in Table 5 and in full in Section D. At t⋆=60t^{\star}=60 months the reduction is not under test, only 1.9%1.9\% of subjects being censored before the horizon, so what the cohort shows is class imbalance rather than censoring. Other-cause death is 5.7%5.7\% of label-complete test subjects and a single threshold covers it 0.2620.262 of the time at a pooled 0.9000.900, while per-class thresholds give 0.8970.897, 0.9000.900 and 0.9000.900 at a mean set size of 1.671.67 against 1.081.08. Membership, a sole registry primary, is settled during follow-up and removes 31%31\% of the breast records, so the guarantee refers to that subpopulation and not to a patient at diagnosis. No guarantee here applies to it numerically either, since censoring depends on the year of diagnosis and the penalty of Theorem 1 is not estimable from the data at hand.

Appendix B Remarks on the theory

Reading Lemma 1’s weight functions.

The weight functions (1,…,1,w⋆)(1,\dots,1,w^{\star}) are the hypothesis of Tibshirani et al.’s Definition 1, not the assignment probabilities they produce. Under their Lemma 3 the case (1,…,1,w)(1,\dots,1,w) collapses to mass proportional to ww on every slot, which is what (5) states. The two displays sit one sentence apart in that lemma and are not two claims about the same object.

Ties. Scores can tie, for instance when the fitted probabilities are constant on groups of covariates. The implementation does not randomise them. It sorts stably and takes the first score whose cumulative weight reaches the target, so tied calibration scores all enter at that point. This is not an assumption of anything proved below. The quantile in (2) is an infimum, so an inclusive convention can only enlarge the set, and every statement in this paper is a coverage floor. Randomisation would be needed for a matching upper bound, which is not claimed.

Remark A2 (Where the weight sits).

Two layers have to be kept apart. At the density layer the assignment computation finds the law of the observed pool proportional to w⋆w^{\star} on the test slot and to 11 on each calibration slot, and at the procedure layer (2) is self-normalised, so a common weight on every slot cancels and amounts to asserting plain exchangeability, which holds within ℐ\mathcal{I} and fails against a population test subject whenever w⋆w^{\star} is not constant. That is the precise sense in which the unweighted procedure on ℐ\mathcal{I} is a guarantee about a different population rather than no guarantee at all. The sign of its bias depends on the joint law of (V,w⋆)(V,w^{\star}), which is what Section 4 varies. The outcome-dependence of w⋆w^{\star} is immaterial here, since Definition 1 and the weighted-quantile lemma ask for absolute continuity, not XX-measurability.

Remark A3 (The atom need not be constant).

Lemma 2 is stated for any dominating atom, so the sharp choice 1/G⁡(t⋆∣X)1/G(t^{\star}\mid X) is covered by it directly, and is no larger than 1/gmin1/g_{\min}. With that atom the mass the calibration fold needs is near the classical 1/α−11/\alpha-1 rather than gmin−1g_{\min}^{-1} times it, so the sharp atom is the better one at known GG.

No plug-in version of that atom is admissible for this lemma, since under an estimated censoring distribution 1/G^​(t⋆∣X)1/\widehat{G}(t^{\star}\mid X) does not dominate 1/G⁡(m∣X)1/G(m\mid X) (Table 4). Under the theorem’s estimated weights the plug-in envelope is the right atom (Lemma 3).

Appendix C The full simulation study

This section gives the rest of the synthetic study.

Design constants.

Pools are 25002500 subjects split in half unless stated, the estimator is a competing-risks forest of 100100 trees in these designs and 200200 on the registry, figures average 2020 replications except Table 13, which averages 2424, Tables 3 and 20, which average 4040, and the tables whose captions give their own count, and the censoring rate is λc=λ​c/(1−c)\lambda_{c}=\lambda\,c/(1-c) for a nominal censoring share cc. The cause-1 hazard is λ1​ex0\lambda_{1}e^{x_{0}} divided by the mean of ex0e^{x_{0}} over the draw, so subjects within one draw are exchangeable rather than independent, through a common factor whose fluctuation is of order n−1/2n^{-1/2}. The true score of Section 4.1 uses the same factor. The calibration pool and the test draw are separate draws with their own factors, so they do not share one law exactly, and in the Weibull and non-proportional families the censoring rate is set from the median latent event time of the draw. These designs are therefore finite-pool illustrations, not exact instances of Assumptions 1 to 3. Table 10 reruns the true-score cells of Table 2 with a fixed normaliser, where the draws are independent and the censoring rate does not depend on them.

Because censoring is covariate-free in these designs, G⁡(t⋆)G(t^{\star}) is fixed by the design, and Assumption 2 permits any gming_{\min} at or below it, which is 0.8410.841, 0.6300.630, 0.3540.354 and 0.1250.125 at censoring 0.20.2, 0.40.4, 0.60.6 and 0.750.75. The designs run at gmin=0.05g_{\min}=0.05, between 2.52.5 and 1717 times looser. That constant is an analyst’s choice. At the atom (3) it enters only through the clip on the calibration weights, which does not bind where those weights are the oracle ones. Where censoring depends on the covariates, as in Table 12, G⁡(t⋆∣X)G(t^{\star}\mid X) is not a constant.

Two evaluators.

Inside the assumptions coverage is computed against the generating process’s closed-form censoring survival, so the evaluation shares no estimate with the procedure. Where positivity fails an oracle-weighted estimate is itself biased, so coverage is computed directly against the latent label. The one place that disagreement changed a claim is reported below.

Estimating the weights.

Table 12 drives the censoring model away from the truth by making the censoring hazard depend on a covariate with strength csc_{s}, and reports the penalty Δw\Delta_{w} alongside the floor it implies. The penalty runs from 0.00350.0035 at cs=0c_{s}=0 to 0.23710.2371 at cs=3c_{s}=3. The unit-atom rows carry no floor, as that table’s caption says. Where there is one, coverage is nowhere below it by more than a standard error. The closest reading is at cs=0c_{s}=0, where Δw\Delta_{w} is 0.00350.0035 and the marginal Kaplan–Meier arm reads 0.8960.896 (SE 0.0030.003) against a floor of 0.8970.897, which is the theorem holding with almost no room. Everywhere else the floor is loose. The floor at cs=3c_{s}=3 is 0.6630.663 against a realised 0.8680.868 for the marginal Kaplan–Meier arm under the capped oracle-weight evaluator, or 0.8300.830 under the direct latent-label evaluator of Table 12, which scores the positivity-violating subjects the cap hides. The conclusion holds under either, and the size of the gap does not. The latent-label evaluator is the stricter of the two.

The rows divide at the point where positivity fails. The population mass with G⁡(t⋆∣X)<gminG(t^{\star}\mid X)<g_{\min} is estimated from 200,000200{,}000 draws of the data-generating process, and it runs 00, 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, 0.0190.019, 0.1270.127 and 0.2000.200 across the grid, which is 00, 22, 3,8493{,}849, 25,48225{,}482 and 40,07340{,}073 of those draws. Assumption 2 is almost-sure, so anything above zero is a violation, but the second entry is two draws and no estimate from this many can tell it from zero. We therefore treat cs≥1c_{s}\geq 1, where the estimate is more than five of its own standard errors from zero, as outside the assumptions. At cs=0.5c_{s}=0.5 the estimate cannot be told from zero, which does not establish the almost-sure bound, so we report cs=0.5c_{s}=0.5 next to cs=0c_{s}=0 without claiming it satisfies Assumption 2. Every arm is valid at cs=1c_{s}=1, a property of that design rather than of the assumption.

Outside positivity.

At cs=3c_{s}=3 the conditional-forest arm reads 0.9100.910 under the capped evaluator but 0.8740.874 against the latent label, and the unweighted arm moves the same way, 0.8790.879 to 0.8410.841. The capped evaluator cannot see the fifth of the population that defines the failure. Outside the assumption the weighting rescues nothing.

The rate.

Under the joint-independence hypothesis of Corollary 1 the penalty decays at a fitted log-log slope of −0.497-0.497 over nn from 500500 to 32,00032{,}000 (Table 13). Under the conditional hypothesis, where a marginal estimator does not converge to G(⋅∣X)G(\cdot\mid X), it is flat at 0.1070.107 over the same range. The corollary needs the branch it names.

Where the crossing is, and how well we locate it.

Table 3 runs the grid at 4040 replications and Table 18 reruns it at 250250 on a six-point bb grid, against a bar of |t|≥4\lvert t\rvert\geq 4 fixed before the run. Table 17 locates the crossing itself. Resampling the same replications, the interpolated b∗b^{\ast} runs from 0.3190.319 to 0.5570.557. How that compares with the misspecification an analyst commits without a dial has to be asked inside one family at a time, because that mistake is not the same size in all three. The smallest crossing here, 0.3190.319 under non-proportional hazards at censoring 0.200.20, falls in the family where that mistake is largest, and that pairing is not separated from zero. The bootstrap interval at exponential hazards and censoring 0.200.20 is [0.460,0.575][0.460,0.575], wider than the grid spacing of 0.10.1, which is the condition fixed beforehand for saying that 250250 replications do not resolve a location. And the contour rises with the censoring rate in the Weibull and non-proportional families, +0.134+0.134 with [+0.088,+0.178][+0.088,+0.178] and +0.185+0.185 with [+0.145,+0.233][+0.145,+0.233], but not in the exponential one, where the paired rise is +0.038+0.038 with [−0.016,+0.093][-0.016,+0.093].

Further sweeps.

Appendix K reports the remaining sweeps: the ceiling under oracle weights, a set read directly off the fitted model, the searches for an unweighted failure at a fitted score across censoring rates, the event-free share and an uninformative score, and a violation of independent censoring by the latent cause.

The guarantee does not depend on the score.

Validity is distribution-free in the nonconformity score, and Table 15 confirms it across three event-time families crossed with a misspecification dial. The paper’s score holds at 0.8980.898 to 0.9020.902 in all fifteen cells even where the fitted model has never seen the covariate the data generating process uses. Section G gives the design.

Appendix D A registry cohort

At t⋆=60t^{\star}=60 months only 1.94%1.94\% of subjects are censored before the horizon, the censoring weights are flat, and the weighted and unweighted procedures agree to 0.0020.002 in coverage, so at that horizon the cohort does not test the weighting. Section A.1 uses it for the per-cause gap instead. At t⋆=107t^{\star}=107 months censoring is administrative and depends on the year of diagnosis, so a marginal Kaplan–Meier is a misspecified censoring model and a year-stratified one is available. That makes the cohort a real-data counterpart of the comparison in Section 4.3. No guarantee of Section 3 applies here numerically, since the penalty of Theorem 1 is a population quantity in the unknown GG, so the figures below are measurements.

Marginal and year-stratified censoring models at t⋆=107t^{\star}=107. The year-stratified model fits one censoring Kaplan–Meier per diagnosis year on the training fold, with five splits, α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and the same forest and three-way split as the other registry runs (seer-conditional-107.json). The two estimates disagree by 0.720.72 in sup-norm over [0,t⋆][0,t^{\star}] in the worst stratum and by 0.270.27 averaged over the accrual-year distribution. The largest calibration weight rises from 1.261.26 under the marginal model to 13.4013.40 under the stratified one, 1.31%1.31\% of calibration weights are at or above 55, and no weight sits at the gming_{\min} clip.

Pooled coverage is 0.91260.9126 unweighted, 0.90040.9004 under the marginal weights and 0.89920.8992 under the stratified ones, at mean set sizes of 1.351.35, 1.281.28 and 1.281.28. The three arms share splits, forest and scores, so the gap of 0.01340.0134 between the first and the last decomposes. Weighting at all accounts for 0.01230.0123 of it, and correcting the censoring model accounts for 0.00110.0011, about one standard error of either arm over the five splits. Scoring all three arms under a year-stratified coverage estimator instead of the marginal one moves pooled coverage by at most 0.00060.0006. At t⋆=106t^{\star}=106, where the largest weight is 7.07.0, the correction leg is 0.00040.0004. Unlike Section 4.3, the marginal model is the one closer to nominal here, and the two models differ by about a thousandth, because their disagreement is concentrated in a class whose labels are nearly homogeneous. The censoring estimator removes a failure from the censoring risk set before a censoring recorded in the same month, as the convention T≤CT\leq C requires.

Positivity at t⋆=107t^{\star}=107 holds by one month. The minimum accrual-year stratum censoring survival is 0.0770.077 against gmin=0.05g_{\min}=0.05, the smallest G^\widehat{G} any evaluated subject carries is 0.07470.0747, and at t⋆=120t^{\star}=120 on the full cohort no follow-up in the 2014 and 2015 strata reaches the horizon, so their censoring survival is 00. A per-year minimum averages within the year, so it is a coarser check than Assumption 2 requires.

Cohort construction. The cohort is SEER Research Data, 17 Registries, November 2025 submission (2000–2023), breast cancer restricted to patients for whom it is their sole registry primary and to diagnosis years 2010–2015. The sole-primary restriction makes the two causes well defined and keeps 991,122991{,}122 of 1,442,0831{,}442{,}083 breast records. Whether a second primary appears is settled during follow-up, so the analysed population is the patients whose breast cancer remains their only primary, not patients at diagnosis, and the restriction is a named mechanism against Assumption 1. Two further filters depend on the outcome. Deaths of unknown cause (1,4911{,}491, 0.60%0.60\%) and records whose survival time is not computed from complete dates (7,3577{,}357, 2.98%2.98\%) are removed. The analysed cohort has 238,057238{,}057 subjects, of whom 37,73537{,}735 died of the cancer, 31,33031{,}330 of other causes and 168,992168{,}992 were alive or censored at last follow-up. Recoding the removed records in four ways, from reinstating them under their recorded status to recoding every death as censored, moves the per-cause coverages under the pooled threshold at t⋆=60t^{\star}=60 within [0.557,0.588][0.557,0.588] for cancer death and [0.247,0.275][0.247,0.275] for other-cause death, and pooled coverage stays in [0.8996,0.9001][0.8996,0.9001]. All 4,6074{,}607 subjects censored before 6060 months are recorded alive, so censoring at that horizon is loss to follow-up, and Assumption 1 there is untested.

D.1 Public cohorts

Three competing-risks cohorts ship with the R package survival. The rows of Table 6 run the same code at the same α\alpha over 200 random splits, at horizons fixed from each cohort’s censoring distribution before any coverage was computed.

Coverage here is estimated under the marginal censoring model the weighted procedure calibrates on, so the estimates do not establish population coverage. Under this estimator the unweighted procedure is estimated above nominal in every cell, by 0.0030.003 to 0.0290.029, and the weighted one returns smaller sets in all 6. That model is wrong here. Censoring depends on the year of diagnosis in mgus2 and of sampling in FLC. Within quartiles of that year the censoring survival at the later horizon of mgus2 runs 0.9930.993, 1.0001.000, 0.9150.915 and 0.0430.043, and of FLC 0.9440.944, 1.0001.000, 0.8560.856 and 0.0000.000, so the latest quarter of accrual lies outside Assumption 2 in both. PBC, stratified by albumin, stays at or above 0.3660.366.

Applying the shrinkage bb of Section 4.2 moves the unweighted procedure and, under this evaluator, not the weighted one. At b=0.6b=0.6 mgus2 at 134134 months reads 0.89130.8913, 5.05.0 standard errors below nominal, against 0.90060.9006 weighted, and PBC at 2,1692{,}169 days reads 0.89660.8966 against 0.90340.9034, 1.01.0 standard error below nominal with 399399 subjects. The paired contrast between the arms changes sign under the shrinkage, from +0.0119+0.0119 at b=0b=0 to −0.0067-0.0067 at b=0.6b=0.6 on PBC and from +0.0016+0.0016 to −0.0093-0.0093 on mgus2. At b=0.6b=0.6 the mgus2 model predicts an event-free rate of 0.1210.121 where the complete cases show 0.3020.302, so this is a stress test.

Dang et al. (2026) report 14.3%14.3\% coverage on PBC under complete-case conformal calibration. Their calibration keeps only subjects with an observed event, so the subjects event-free at the horizon, the group Section 4.2 finds decisive, are absent from it rather than under-represented, and they predict an interval on an event time rather than a set of causes.

Proof.

Both YY and m=min⁡(T,t⋆)m=\min(T,t^{\star}) are functions of (T,ε)(T,\varepsilon). Conditioning on (T,ε,X)(T,\varepsilon,X) and using Assumption 1, 𝔼[Δ∣T,ε,X]=ℙ(C≥m∣X)=G(m∣X)=1/w⋆\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mid T,\varepsilon,X]=\mathbb{P}(C\geq m\mid X)=G(m\mid X)=1/w^{\star}, so 𝔼[Δw⋆h∣T,ε,X]=h\mathbb{E}[\Delta w^{\star}h\mid T,\varepsilon,X]=h. Take expectations. ∎

Proof of Lemma 1.

The assignment claim is that, writing {u0,…,uk}\{u_{0},\dots,u_{k}\} for the conditioned multiset,

ℙ⁡(test slot=ul|multiset,|ℐ|=k)=w⋆​(ul)∑m=0kw⋆​(um),\mathbb{P}\big(\text{test slot}=u_{l}\,\big|\,\text{multiset},\,|\mathcal{I}|=k\big)\;=\;\frac{w^{\star}(u_{l})}{\sum_{m=0}^{k}w^{\star}(u_{m})}, (5)

which is the (1,…,1,w⋆)(1,\dots,1,w^{\star}) structure by Tibshirani et al.’s Lemma 3. Write each subject’s latent tuple ζ=(X,T,ε)\zeta=(X,T,\varepsilon) with law μ\mu. The score V=1−πY​(X)V=1-\pi_{Y}(X) and the weight w⋆=1/G⁡(m∣X)w^{\star}=1/G(m\mid X) are fixed measurable functions of ζ\zeta, and both factor through the observed reduction (X,m,Y)(X,m,Y), so the argument can be read on that pushforward even though ε\varepsilon is not observed when T>t⋆T>t^{\star}. Under Assumption 1, Δ|ζ∼Bernoulli⁡(ρ⁡(ζ))\Delta\mid\zeta\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\rho(\zeta)) independently across subjects, with selection probability

ρ⁡(ζ)≔ℙ⁡(C≥m∣X)=G⁡(m∣X)= 1/w⋆​(ζ).\rho(\zeta)\;\coloneqq\;\mathbb{P}(C\geq m\mid X)\;=\;G(m\mid X)\;=\;1/w^{\star}(\zeta).

Put q=𝔼⁡[ρ⁡(ζ)]=ℙ⁡(Δ=1)q=\mathbb{E}[\rho(\zeta)]=\mathbb{P}(\Delta=1).

Assignment ratio. Fix |ℐ|=k|\mathcal{I}|=k and the observed multiset, and compare the labelling that puts u0u_{0} in the test slot, with density fAf_{A}, against the one that puts u1u_{1} there, with density fBf_{B}. A test slot contributes the plain density μ⁡(u)\mu(u). Each retained calibration slot contributes ρ⁡(u)​μ​(u)\rho(u)\mu(u). The n−kn-k censored calibration slots integrate over their unobserved values to the common factor (1−q)n−k(1-q)^{n-k}, and the slot and order choices are common to both labellings. Hence

fA∝μ⁡(u0)​∏j=1kρ⁡(uj)​μ​(uj),fB∝μ⁡(u1)​ρ​(u0)​μ​(u0)​∏j=2kρ⁡(uj)​μ​(uj),f_{A}\propto\mu(u_{0})\prod_{j=1}^{k}\rho(u_{j})\mu(u_{j}),\qquad f_{B}\propto\mu(u_{1})\,\rho(u_{0})\mu(u_{0})\prod_{j=2}^{k}\rho(u_{j})\mu(u_{j}),

The random size of ℐ\mathcal{I}. Under independent Bernoulli⁡(ρ⁡(ζi))\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\rho(\zeta_{i})) selection over i.i.d. subjects, the size and the retained values factorise. |ℐ|∼Binomial⁡(n,q)|\mathcal{I}|\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,q), and given any selection pattern with kk ones the retained tuples are i.i.d. from Qsel∝ρ​d​μQ_{\mathrm{sel}}\propto\rho\,\mathrm{d}\mu, the same law for every pattern, while each censored subject contributes the value-free constant 1−q1-q. Proof of Lemma 2.

With the oracle test atom wte⋆w^{\star}_{\mathrm{te}} the floor is exactly Lemma 1. Proof of Corollary 1.

Proof.

Under joint independence G⁡(u∣X)=G⁡(u)G(u\mid X)=G(u) and the marginal Kaplan–Meier estimator does not depend on XX, so supu≤t⋆|G^​(u)−G⁡(u)|\sup_{u\leq t^{\star}}|\widehat{G}(u)-G(u)| is a constant given 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} and the expectation in the bound of Theorem 1 has nothing random left inside it, since Δw≤gmin−2​supu≤t⋆|G^​(u)−G⁡(u)|\Delta_{w}\leq g_{\min}^{-2}\sup_{u\leq t^{\star}}|\widehat{G}(u)-G(u)|. The rate is in the size of the training fold, on which G^\widehat{G} is fitted, and not in the calibration count of Lemma 1. ∎

Proof of Corollary 2.

Proof.

Condition on Y=ℓY=\ell throughout. The calibration subjects with Yi=ℓY_{i}=\ell and a test subject with Y=ℓY=\ell are i.i.d. draws from μℓ=μ(⋅∣Y=ℓ)\mu_{\ell}=\mu(\cdot\mid Y=\ell), because YY is a function of the latent tuple ζ\zeta and the subjects are i.i.d. Selection is unchanged by the conditioning. Given ζ\zeta, Δ\Delta is Bernoulli⁡(ρ⁡(ζ))\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\rho(\zeta)) independently across subjects by Assumption 1, and ρ⁡(ζ)=G⁡(m∣X)≥gmin\rho(\zeta)=G(m\mid X)\geq g_{\min} by Assumption 2, both of which hold pointwise in ζ\zeta and therefore on μℓ\mu_{\ell}. Lemma 1 applies verbatim with μ\mu replaced by μℓ\mu_{\ell}, giving weighted exchangeability of ℐℓ\mathcal{I}_{\ell} together with the test subject under the same weight functions, and the argument of Theorem 1 follows with every expectation taken under μℓ\mu_{\ell}. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.

Proof.

The two lemmas differ in which procedure carries the exact floor, so they differ in what the atom substitutes for. In Lemma 2 the floor is Lemma 1, whose weighted-quantile step puts wte⋆w^{\star}_{\mathrm{te}} on the test slot, and the atom replaces that. In Theorem 1 the floor is not transported from that procedure. Lei and Candès prove their lower bound by introducing the tilted law P~\widetilde{P} with d​P~=r^​d​Qsel\mathrm{d}\widetilde{P}=\widehat{r}\,\mathrm{d}Q_{\mathrm{sel}}, under which the estimate is the true ratio, applying the weighted-quantile inequality there, and only then transporting to PP at cost dTV​(P,P~)=12​𝔼Qsel​|r^−r⋆|=Δwd_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widetilde{P})=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{Q_{\mathrm{sel}}}|\widehat{r}-r^{\star}|=\Delta_{w}. Read on the multiset of Lemma 1, the exact step is ∑lp^l​𝟏​{El}≥1−α\sum_{l}\widehat{p}_{l}\mathbf{1}\{E_{l}\}\geq 1-\alpha with p^l∝w^​(ul)\widehat{p}_{l}\propto\widehat{w}(u_{l}), and the transport replaces p^\widehat{p} by pl⋆∝w⋆​(ul)p^{\star}_{l}\propto w^{\star}(u_{l}) at cost their total variation. So the slot the atom stands in for carries w^te\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{te}} and not wte⋆w^{\star}_{\mathrm{te}}, and normalisation is common to every slot and cancels. There is no route to ∑lpl⋆​𝟏​{El}≥1−α\sum_{l}p^{\star}_{l}\mathbf{1}\{E_{l}\}\geq 1-\alpha directly, because ElE_{l} is decided by a threshold computed at w^\widehat{w}. Atom mass only inflates the quantile, so any A≥w^teA\geq\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{te}} preserves the floor, exactly as in Lemma 2.

For (i), m=min⁡(T,t⋆)≤t⋆m=\min(T,t^{\star})\leq t^{\star} and G^(⋅∣X)\widehat{G}(\cdot\mid X) is non-increasing, so max⁡{G^​(t⋆∣X),gmin}≤max⁡{G^​(m∣X),gmin}\max\{\widehat{G}(t^{\star}\mid X),g_{\min}\}\leq\max\{\widehat{G}(m\mid X),g_{\min}\}, and the same G^\widehat{G} supplies both sides, which is what makes the inequality exact rather than statistical. An envelope built from a different estimator than the one supplying the weights carries no such guarantee. For (ii), the implementation calibrates with 1/max⁡(G^,gmin)1/\max(\widehat{G},g_{\min}), so w^≤1/gmin\widehat{w}\leq 1/g_{\min} pointwise with no condition. Corollary 2 inherits the statement, its proof taking every expectation under μℓ\mu_{\ell} and touching the atom only through Lemma 1. ∎

Appendix F Reading the numbers

Remark A4 (What pushes the weighted procedure up).

Two forces push coverage up. The atom in (2) adds mass p∞=A/(∑jw^j+A)p_{\infty}=A/(\sum_{j}\widehat{w}_{j}+A) before the quantile target is reached, so q^\widehat{q} is inflated, and that mass grows as the calibration fold gets smaller. And Theorem 1 is one-sided. With a correct censoring model and folds of the size used here the push is small: Section 4 finds the weighted procedure within 0.0120.012 of nominal on either side, with 1212 of the 2424 weighted cells of Table 3 below 0.9000.900 before rounding, so neither direction is evidence for or against exactness.

Checking the operating condition.

The condition of Remark A1 can be checked before any set is formed. Fix gming_{\min} first, below the minimum of G^​(t⋆∣X)\widehat{G}(t^{\star}\mid X) over the covariate support with a margin, then compute W=∑i∈ℐw^iW=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\widehat{w}_{i} on the calibration fold and compare it with A⁡(1−α)/αA(1-\alpha)/\alpha for the atom the procedure carries. At (3) that boundary runs 2.82.8 to 155.4155.4 over the sweep of Figure 4, and it is 9.29.2 on the registry cohort. If WW falls short, enlarge the calibration fold, or in the class-conditional version report the causes below the boundary as uninformative. Raising gming_{\min} after seeing WW satisfies the condition on paper and removes the floor it protects.

Selection and the direction of the bias.

At censoring 0.750.75 the mean score among label-complete test subjects is 0.6490.649 against 0.4360.436 over all test subjects, so label-completeness selects the harder subjects and a threshold calibrated for the population is too small for that subgroup. At censoring 0.20.2 the same gap is 0.5480.548 against 0.5340.534 and the coverage gap closes with it.

That mean shift is a guide to the direction and not what decides it. The unweighted threshold is the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of the label-complete scores, so the procedure under-covers exactly when the population puts less than 1−α1-\alpha of its mass at or below that point, which depends on the joint law of (V,w⋆)(V,w^{\star}) (Remark A2) and not on a summary of it. Three covariate groups make the gap concrete (e56_mean_shift.py). The first, of mass 0.20.2, fails early from cause 11, so its score is 00, and is selected with probability 0.050.05. The second, of mass 0.20.2, fails early from either cause with probability 1/21/2, scores 0.50.5 and is never censored. The third, of mass 0.60.6, has π=(0.8,0.2,0)\pi=(0.8,0.2,0) and is selected with probability 0.050.05. Every selection probability is at least gmin=0.05g_{\min}=0.05 and the score is the truth. Label-complete subjects are harder on average, with mean score 0.4570.457 against 0.2920.292, yet selection piles their mass on the second group’s 0.50.5, the unweighted threshold falls from the population’s 0.80.8 to 0.50.5, and coverage over the population is 0.880.88 against 0.900.90. The other experiments agree. In the exact search of Appendix H, a downward shift of the score distribution under selection accompanies 2,4642{,}464 of the 2,6382{,}638 failing (law, α\alpha) pairs, the cruder proxy that the most probable label is also the earliest holds in 1,9401{,}940, and the rule that the sign of the shift is opposite to the correlation between censoring hazard and expected nonconformity holds at γ=+3\gamma=+3 and fails at γ=−3\gamma=-3 (Table 8).

Appendix G Further detail

The score-misspecification design.

Table 15 crosses three event-time families with a misspecification dial λ\lambda. The families are exponential, Weibull with the two causes given qualitatively different baseline hazards, and one where the cause-1 covariate effect reverses at a knot. The dial corrupts what the model is trained on, replacing the informative covariate by 1−λ​x0+λ​z\sqrt{1-\lambda}\,x_{0}+\sqrt{\lambda}\,z with zz independent noise of the same variance, and then applies the fitted model to the true covariates at calibration and test time. At λ=1\lambda=1 the model has never seen the covariate the data generating process uses. The paper’s score holds at 0.8980.898 to 0.9020.902 across all fifteen cells, and an adaptive-set score with randomisation holds at 0.9000.900 to 0.9040.904. The same score without randomisation returns the whole label space in every cell, at coverage 1.0001.000 and set size 3.003.00, a low-cardinality degeneracy of non-randomised adaptive sets and not a property of censoring.

Appendix H A law where unweighted calibration fails at the true score

The label-complete calibration subjects and a label-complete test subject are exchangeable, so the unweighted procedure is valid for the label-complete subpopulation. The weighting changes the population the guarantee is about. We prefer the population because whether a subject will be followed to their label turns on a censoring time that has not happened yet, so the label-complete subgroup cannot be identified at prediction time. The design below shows that the unweighted procedure can fail over the population inside the assumptions and at the true score.

Take two equal covariate groups at t⋆=1t^{\star}=1 with α=0.2\alpha=0.2 and exponential censoring independent of XX with G⁡(t⋆)=0.082G(t^{\star})=0.082, above the gmin=0.05g_{\min}=0.05 the procedure is configured with, so Assumption 2 holds. Group 00 fails early, at a time uniform on (0.02,0.30)(0.02,0.30), always from cause 11, so its true π\pi is a point mass and its score is 00. Group 11’s event time is uniform on (0.96,1.04)(0.96,1.04) and it fails from cause 11 with probability 0.80.8, so its true (π0,π1,π2)(\pi_{0},\pi_{1},\pi_{2}) is (0.5,0.4,0.1)(0.5,0.4,0.1) and its m=min⁡(T,t⋆)m=\min(T,t^{\star}) is within 0.040.04 of the horizon. The score is the true π\pi, which is what Theorem 1 conditions on.

Label-completeness keeps 0.680.68 of group 00 and 0.0840.084 of group 11, so 0.890.89 of the calibration sample is the group whose score is 00, more than the 1−α=0.81-\alpha=0.8 the quantile needs, and the unweighted 1−α1-\alpha quantile is 00 with it. Over the population, scored against the latent label on every test subject, the unweighted procedure covers 0.4990.499 against a nominal 0.8000.800, at a mean set size of 0.500.50 of 33. Below the threshold it returns the empty set, and on group 11 it covers nothing at all. The weights are 1/G⁡(m)1/G(m), which is between 1.051.05 and 2.122.12 on group 00 and between 11.011.0 and 12.212.2 on group 11, and they restore that group’s mass, and the weighted procedure covers 0.9500.950 at q^=0.600\widehat{q}=0.600. What that threshold buys is the point. On group 00 it returns the single correct label, and on group 11, the only subjects whose label at t⋆t^{\star} is in doubt, it returns two labels of three and covers 0.9000.900. Inside the assumptions, the unweighted procedure fails and the weighted one is informative about exactly the subjects the failure concerns.

The size-22 set is available only because group 11’s two causes are not equally likely. With probability 1/21/2 each the two causes tie in score, no threshold admits one without the other, and the weighted set on group 11 is the whole label space. That version is the control, over two hundred replications.

The figures above use the closed-form GG, so on their own they exhibit Lemma 2 rather than Theorem 1. Refitting the weights from a Kaplan–Meier estimate on an independent training fold, which is the regime the theorem covers, the exhibit survives, at coverage 0.9480.948 and a group-11 set size of 1.9901.990 against 0.9500.950 and 2.0002.000 at the oracle weights.

The mechanism is the one Remark A2 names. Here selection over-represents the zero-score group, so the label-complete quantile sits below the population’s and the unweighted threshold is too small. The same comparison drives Section 4.1, where the true score under-covers once few subjects are event-free at the horizon, and Section 4.3, where it fails between two regions. The guarantee is what covers both signs.

The failure is not confined to constructed corners. An exhaustive exact search over 5,9855{,}985 three-label laws with fixed failure times, the true score and covariate-free censoring, each at four levels α\alpha, finds 2,6382{,}638 of the 23,94023{,}940 pairs, from 1,6451{,}645 laws, in which the unweighted procedure covers below nominal, the worst at 0.4000.400 against a nominal 0.800.80 (cr-counterexample.py).

The two-point example below is the same phenomenon at its degenerate end, and the contrast is the reason the design above needs three labels and a covariate. With two labels, no covariate and a marginal probability below 1−α1-\alpha, no non-randomised set short of the whole space exists at any threshold, so the triviality is a fact about the target and not about anything a procedure chose. The design above escapes it because three labels and an asymmetric cause split put a set of size 22 inside the score space to begin with. With T∼Exp⁡(1)T\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1), C∼Exp⁡(1.5)C\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1.5) at t⋆=1t^{\star}=1 and no covariates, label-complete selection moves the probability of the early-failure label from 0.6320.632 to 0.8170.817 and the unweighted procedure covers 0.6320.632 against a nominal 0.800.80. Its weighted set is the whole label space, since P⁡(Y=1)=0.632<0.8P(Y=1)=0.632<0.8.

Appendix J Further tables

Appendix K Further simulation results

These sweeps complement Appendix C and use its design constants.

The ceiling.

Under oracle weights the procedure sits at nominal, and the realisable atom’s cost is a property of the constant chosen for it (Table 26).

Reading a set off the fitted model.

Without any calibration, a set can be read off the fitted cumulative incidence functions by ordering the labels by π^ℓ​(x)\hat{\pi}_{\ell}(x) and taking the smallest prefix whose fitted mass reaches 1−α1-\alpha. The last row of each block of Table 22 is that set, on the same forest, split and test fold as the rows above it. It over-covers only because with three labels a prefix has to overshoot. Splitting the boundary label with one uniform draw per subject removes the overshoot, and the set then covers 0.8820.882 down to 0.8460.846 across the censoring grid at 2.212.21 to 2.042.04 labels, against 0.9040.904 to 0.9110.911 at 2.312.31 to 2.392.39 labels for the weighted procedure.

Five searches for an unweighted failure, four at a fitted score.

None found the unweighted procedure below nominal inside the assumptions. Four score with the fitted forest: across censoring rates (Table 23), on the in-assumption rows of covariate-dependent censoring (Table 12), across the event-free share (Table 24) and across the miscoverage level crossed with four censoring rates (Figure 4). The forest overstates the event-free probability, which pushes the unweighted procedure up, so these describe the procedure at that fit rather than at a correct one. Section 4.1 reruns three of them at the true score, where the share search finds under-coverage. The fifth, on bounded covariate-dependent censoring, uses the true score and holds, lowest at 0.90080.9008 (Table 8). Crossing an uninformative score with a minority event-free label, again at a fitted score, the unweighted procedure covers 0.9110.911 against a nominal 0.9000.900 (Table 25).

When the assumptions fail.

Positivity is handled in Section 4.3 and Table 14. For independent censoring, Table 27 multiplies the censoring hazard by ecce^{c_{c}} for subjects whose latent cause is the first one. Pooled coverage stays within 0.0160.016 of nominal while cause-1 coverage under a single threshold falls from 0.8210.821 to 0.6810.681, and the unweighted arm tracks the weighted one to within 0.0240.024 on cause-1. Per-cause thresholds hold cause-1 at 0.9320.932 to 0.9450.945 across the sweep and pay in the event-free group, 0.8870.887 at cc=3c_{c}=3. These per-cause thresholds use the constant atom 1/gmin1/g_{\min}. Conditioning on a named cause makes censoring independent within that cause in this construction, but the shared marginal censoring estimate is not the right model for each class, and the event-free group is not a named cause, so these readings are measurements of this design and not a consequence of Corollary 2.
